newsitem.title: UK: Christopher to meet British, French leaders on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Christopher to meet British, French leaders on Iraq.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Thursday meets British officials who have backed attacks on Iraq and then flies to Paris for talks with French leaders who have balked at Washington's latest intervention in the Gulf.

Although Iraq has dominated the headlines on Christopher's five-day trip to London, Paris, Bonn and Stuttgart, which began Wednesday, there are also other items on his agenda, including the Bosnian elections, NATO enlargement, and the Middle East.

Britain has supported the United States fully in its decision to mount two air strikes on Iraq this week in retaliation for President Saddam Hussein's recent action against Kurdish-controlled areas in northern Iraq.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters the United States believes there are credible reports that Saddam's forces killed 100 Kurds last Saturday and Sunday.

Britain has also backed the United States in extending the limit of the air-exclusion zone in southern Iraq to the 33rd parallel, on the outskirts of Baghdad, from the 32nd parallel where it was fixed after Iraq's defeat in the 1991 Gulf War.

But France -- another close NATO ally -- has criticised the air strikes and not joined the expanded non-fly operation, even though it has been a critical part of enforcing the scheme in the previously more restricted area.

Christopher is due to have breakfast with British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and then fly to Paris for lunch and talks with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette. He is also to meet President Jacques Chirac before heading for Bonn.
The secretary said on Wednesday he hoped to persuade France to join the United States and Britain in patrolling an expanded no-fly zone in Iraq.

"The cooperation of the French on this is highly desirable. They have been a very important partner in this (Gulf War- originated) coalition and we hope they will continue to participate fully in these matters," Christopher said.

U.S. President Bill Clinton expanded the air exclusion zone on Tuesday as part of an operation that included two air strikes against Iraq in retaliation for its incursion into Kurdish controlled areas in northern Iraq.

Christopher said France objected to the U.S. air strikes against Iraq for legal reasons. He planned to explain to French leaders the U.S. rationale for the attacks, including an insistence that Iraqi President Saddam Hussein "pay a price" for his aggression against Kurds and that the airspace in the no-fly zones be made safer for allied pilots.
Christopher described a planned speech on Friday in Stuttgart on European security as the centrepiece of his trip.

Other topics of discussion with allied leaders include September 14 elections in Bosnia whose legitimacy is already being questioned, disputes over treatment of U.S.-dubbed "rogue states" Iran and Cuba and Russia's ties to NATO.
